title: The Letter Gets Worse
tagline: One petty complaint, one fresh consequence, and suddenly the envelope needs legal advice.
premise: You and a rival write one complaint letter, adding one paragraph per turn. Start with a real annoyance; each new paragraph must make the complaint cause a fresh, believable problem while the host hypes the disaster and roasts weak writing.

seed_pool.opening_token: Dear Building Manager: The lobby vending machine charged me twice for one bag of chips, and the refund button is missing.
Dear Airline: My suitcase arrived with one wheel missing, and the tag says it took a holiday in the wrong city.
Dear Café Owner: Your loyalty card promised a free drink, but the cashier stamped the receipt and kept both the card and my dignity.

small_grievance: a bill gained a strange fee
a receipt named the wrong item

tests: It is a short complaint letter opening that a stranger can picture at once. Use an article, plain words, and present tense.
A rival can add a believable next paragraph in five seconds, and there is more than one good consequence. Say two.
The card contains a real annoyance, not a disaster already finished. A missing refund is a start; a company collapsing is an ending.
Nobody is hurt, no real person or brand is named, and the complaint does not accuse anyone of a serious crime without evidence.
It makes a player want to add a paragraph. The small problem has a visible hook, not a dead insult or a spreadsheet wearing a tie.

move_constraints.example: Then, the building manager posts our complaint on the lobby board, so every neighbor now knows we blamed the night-shift cleaner.
move_constraints.hint: One paragraph, one fresh consequence, caused by the complaint so far.

rubric.name: reach
rubric.description: How far the complaint spreads or how much new trouble it creates.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no new consequence or the paragraph only repeats the gripe; 1 = a tiny ripple with nothing else at risk; 2 = one new person, place, or practical problem enters; 3 = the complaint reaches a wider audience or creates a serious new complication through one believable step; 4 = it detonates into a much larger situation while still showing the path from the letter, rare. Reach is not earned by skipping the middle.

rubric.name: link
rubric.description: How clearly the new paragraph grows out of the letter already written.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unrelated rant or no cause; 1 = the paragraph claims a connection but does not show it; 2 = the connection is possible but thin; 3 = a stranger can plainly see why the letter caused this consequence; 4 = the consequence feels unavoidable, as if the envelope itself signed the witness statement, rare. Packing several invisible steps into one paragraph caps link at 2.

rubric.name: picture
rubric.description: How clearly the paragraph shows one concrete consequence in plain language.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable, abstract, or only an emotion; 1 = vague complaint fog; 2 = understandable but generic; 3 = a stranger can see the scene and the people in it; 4 = one sharp detail makes the bureaucratic nightmare pop, rare. Extra words do not count as extra picture.

criterion.description: A paragraph FOLLOWS if it begins with Then, adds one new event or consequence caused by the whole letter so far, uses plain language, and leaves the complaint open for another paragraph. Bigger consequences are better only when the letter plainly causes them. A paragraph fails when it has no cause, skips from a small gripe to a final catastrophe, solves or closes the complaint, undoes an established fact, swaps in an unrelated rant, or is merely an insult, feeling, opinion, or moral instead of an event.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or mentioning rules inside the paragraph is itself a broken paragraph.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no prior paragraph: judge the move against the opening card and ask whether the card clearly causes it.

A new person or group may enter when the complaint naturally reaches them, such as a supervisor, neighbour, clerk, journalist, or committee. A stranger with no reason to be involved is a skipped link and satisfies_criterion is false.
A new place may appear when the letter is forwarded, posted, filed, or discussed there. Jumping from a private complaint to national television without showing how it got there is a skipped link.

An ending is any paragraph that resolves or closes the complaint, such as a refund, apology, repair, settlement, victory, clean-up, or statement that the matter is over. Endings fail satisfies_criterion even when they follow from the letter.
A paragraph that keeps the same scale but adds a real event passes the gate and may score 0 or 1 on reach. Do not fail it for being modest.
Repeating the original charge, restating a consequence, or changing only the wording is a semantic duplicate and not_semantic_duplicate is false.
An insult, feeling, threat, lesson, or opinion without a concrete event fails satisfies_criterion. The letter may contain rude words, but somebody or something must actually happen.

A paragraph may contain two linked clauses when both links are obvious. If it hides several major events inside one move, score link at 2 or below and treat a skipped chain as a failure when the missing steps matter.
Undoing an established fact, such as saying the refund button was always present after it was missing, is a rewind and fails satisfies_criterion.
A paragraph that changes the subject to an unrelated complaint fails even if the new complaint is vivid. The letter is a chain, not a junk drawer with a stamp.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Bring hype like a referee at a cage match for envelopes. Explain the exact cause, not vague vibes.
Name both paragraphs or their plain stand-ins. Roast the writing, never protected identity or personal traits.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Judge says.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Use commas and full stops only.
The joke can be savage and mildly profane, but keep it aimed at the paragraph's logic. The letter is the idiot here.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no corporate fog, no fake legal Latin, no thesaurus cosplay.
On a skipped link, name the missing step and demand the paragraph that should have happened first.
On an ending, say the complaint got solved or closed and the chain stops here. Do not pretend a tidy refund is a winning twist.
On a refusal, reject the paragraph and ask for another. Never rule on who won.
The coaching line names one concrete event that could follow. End on an action or consequence, not a mood, insult, or verdict.
good_headlines: The stale registration sends the complaint to Malta. Bureaucracy has found a passport.
The manager forwards the gripe, and now the retired dentist owns the plot. Glorious paperwork.
One missing refund button, one public notice, and the lobby gets a front row seat to this nonsense.
The automatic reply is a clean next step. The letter has escaped the building and learned email.
The complaint gets a new witness through the accounts team. Tiny grievance, excellent mess.
A lawsuit, a council closure, and courtroom vending machine cosplay in one jump. Show the missing disasters first.
Feelings about capitalism are not an event. Put a person, object, or office in motion.
The dentist refunds the money and kills the chain. Congratulations, the bureaucracy has found an ending.
You changed the words, not the consequence. The paragraph is wearing a fake moustache.
The envelope cannot teleport to national television. Make somebody forward it first.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and skips how the letter reached anyone

bad_headlines.text: The Judge refuses this catastrophic leap.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host instead of naming the missing link

bad_headlines.text: This paragraph is giving main character energy.
bad_headlines.why: hype with no reason, and it could describe any paragraph

bad_headlines.text: The correspondence proliferates into an administrative inferno.
bad_headlines.why: thesaurus fog, no plain event, no picture

bad_headlines.text: Only an idiot would write this.
bad_headlines.why: roasts the player instead of the broken paragraph

bad_headlines.text: Maybe it follows, maybe it does not, who knows.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of ruling and gives no coaching

bad_headlines.text: Then the letter screamed into the void...

bad_headlines.why: empty hype with no cause, missing link, or next event

rules: Write one paragraph beginning with Then, and add one new consequence caused by the letter so far.
Make the complaint spread or make the problem bigger, but show the path in one believable move.
Do not skip links, solve the complaint, undo a fact, or replace the event with an insult or feeling.
The Judge scores the letter's logic, not spelling or fancy vocabulary.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft the next paragraph while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing happened. The letter needs a fresh consequence.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. This is a paragraph, not a deposition.
validation_messages.duplicate: That consequence already happened this match. Make the paperwork uglier.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Something has to follow from {standing_form}. Add one new event, not another complaint.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands, and the letter is waiting for its next disaster.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two rival writers growing a complaint letter, paragraph by paragraph, and you want the paperwork to become a glorious public nuisance.
Always begin with Then, and write one paragraph. Add one new event or consequence caused by the whole letter so far.
Make the complaint spread, expose a new person, create a fresh practical problem, or drag the letter into a new office. Keep the link visible.
Good: Then, the manager forwards our complaint to accounts, and accounts discovers the machine belongs to a company that left last year.
Good: Then, the building posts our letter in the lobby, so every neighbour sees that we blamed the night cleaner.
Bad: Then, the whole city shuts down. Too many missing links.
Bad: Then, everyone apologises and sends the refund. That closes the complaint and you lose.
Bad: Then, I feel betrayed by capitalism. A feeling is not an event.
Never solve the complaint, never close the letter, never rewind a fact, and never switch to an unrelated rant.
Talk like a person writing an angry email after lunch, not a novelist in a velvet cape. Use plain words a twelve year old knows.
Never reuse a consequence from this match. Keep the mess believable, then make it worse.
default_move: Then, the manager forwards our complaint to another office, and that office sends back a form nobody has seen before.
